subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Besides Big-O, what do Big-Omega (Ω) and Big-Theta (Θ) notations represent?
reference_answer: Big-O gives an UPPER BOUND: f(n) = O(g(n)) means f grows no faster than g (up to constant factors) for sufficiently large n. Big-Omega gives a LOWER BOUND: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) means f grows at least as fast as g. Big-Theta gives a TIGHT BOUND: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) when f is both O(g) and Ω(g), i.e., f grows at exactly the same rate as g. For example, Merge Sort is Θ(n log n); linear search is O(n) and Ω(1) when considering all cases.
key_points: Big-O: upper bound; Big-Omega: lower bound; Big-Theta: tight bound (both)
Θ(g) means growing at exactly the same order as g

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: What characteristic does an O(log n) algorithm usually have in how it processes data?
reference_answer: An O(log n) algorithm typically shrinks the problem size by a fixed RATIO at each step (e.g., halving), so the number of steps equals the number of times n can be divided by 2 until reaching 1, about log₂ n. Examples: binary search, operations on balanced trees, fast exponentiation. With n = 1 billion, log₂ n is only about 30 steps — doubling the data adds just one step.
key_points: O(log n) arises when each step shrinks the problem by a fixed ratio (often halving)
Doubling the data adds only one step; n = 1 billion needs about 30 steps

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: How does a double-ended queue (Deque) differ from a Stack and a Queue?
reference_answer: A deque allows adding and removing elements at BOTH ends (front and back) in O(1). Thus it generalizes both a Stack (using one end) and a Queue (adding at one end, removing at the other). Deques are used in the sliding-window maximum technique, the 0-1 BFS algorithm, and bounded operation histories.
key_points: A deque allows insertion/removal at both ends in O(1)
It generalizes both Stack and Queue

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Why is a circular queue usually used when implementing a Queue with an array?
reference_answer: With a plain array-based Queue, each dequeue advances the front index, leaving the earlier cells empty and unusable (or requiring an O(n) shift of the whole array). A circular queue treats the array as a ring: the front and rear indices advance modulo the array size ((i + 1) % n), so freed cells are reused and every enqueue/dequeue is O(1).
key_points: A plain array wastes front cells or needs O(n) shifting
A circular queue uses modular indices to reuse cells, with O(1) operations

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: How does a circular linked list differ from an ordinary linked list, and what is it used for?
reference_answer: In a circular linked list, the last node points back to the first node instead of to null, forming a closed loop. It suits rotation problems: the operating system's Round-Robin scheduling (giving the CPU to each process in turn), lists of players taking turns, the Josephus problem. Traversal needs a stop condition of returning to the starting node to avoid an infinite loop.
key_points: The last node points back to the first, forming a loop
Used for rotation: Round-Robin, turn-taking; traversal needs a stop condition

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Implementing a Stack with an array vs a linked list
question: Compare two ways of implementing a Stack: with a (dynamic) array and with a linked list.
reference_answer: With a dynamic array: push/pop at the end are O(1) amortized, data is contiguous so it is CPU-cache friendly with little extra memory; but occasionally the array must grow (O(n) copy). With a linked list: push/pop at the head are always truly O(1) with no resizing, but each element costs extra memory for the pointer and nodes are scattered in memory. In practice, the array-based implementation is usually faster.
key_points: Array: amortized O(1), contiguous memory, occasional resizing
Linked list: true O(1) but pointer overhead and poor cache locality

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Which properties must a binary Min-Heap satisfy?
reference_answer: A binary Min-Heap must satisfy two properties: (1) Shape property — it is a complete binary tree: every level is full except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right. (2) Heap-order property — each node's value is less than or equal to its children's values, so the minimum element is always at the root. Note that a heap imposes no order between siblings (unlike a BST).
key_points: Shape: a complete binary tree
Order: parent ≤ children (min-heap), minimum at the root; no ordering between siblings

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: When inserting an element into a heap and when extracting the root, which operations restore the heap property?
reference_answer: Insertion: place the new element in the last empty position (keeping the complete shape), then 'sift up' — compare with the parent and swap if the order is violated, repeating until correct or reaching the root. Extracting the root: move the last element to the root, then 'sift down' — compare with the smaller child (min-heap) and swap if violated, repeating until correct. Both operations follow a single root-to-leaf path, so they cost O(log n).
key_points: Insert: place at the end then sift up; extract root: move the last element up then sift down
Each operation follows the tree height, O(log n)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Properties of a good hash function
question: What properties should a good hash function for a Hash Table have?
reference_answer: (1) Deterministic: the same key always produces the same hash value. (2) Uniform distribution: keys are spread evenly across buckets, reducing collisions. (3) Fast to compute. (4) Sensitive to changes: slightly different keys (like 'abc' and 'acb') should produce different hash values, using all parts of the key. Hash functions for hash tables do not need the cryptographic properties of secure hash functions.
key_points: Deterministic, uniformly distributed, fast
Uses all parts of the key so similar keys hash differently

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: The Set and Map abstract data types
question: Distinguish the Set and Map (dictionary) abstract data types.
reference_answer: A Set stores a collection of DISTINCT elements, with main operations: add, remove, and test membership. A Map (Dictionary) stores key-value pairs with unique keys, with main operations: assign a value to a key, look up a value by key, delete by key. Both can be implemented with hash tables (HashSet/HashMap, average O(1)) or balanced trees (TreeSet/TreeMap, O(log n), keeping keys ordered).
key_points: Set: distinct elements; Map: key-value pairs with unique keys
Implemented via hash tables (average O(1)) or balanced trees (O(log n), ordered)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Abstract data types (ADT) vs data structures
question: Distinguish an Abstract Data Type (ADT) from a data structure.
reference_answer: An ADT describes a type by its SET OF OPERATIONS and their behavior, without saying how it is implemented — e.g., a Stack is defined by push, pop, top following LIFO. A data structure is a concrete IMPLEMENTATION of an ADT in memory — e.g., a Stack can be implemented with a dynamic array or a linked list. One ADT can have many implementing data structures with different performance.
key_points: ADT: defined by operations and behavior, independent of implementation
Data structure: how an ADT is realized in memory; one ADT, many implementations

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: What three steps make up the Divide and Conquer strategy? Name some algorithms using it.
reference_answer: Three steps: (1) Divide — split the problem into smaller subproblems of the same form; (2) Conquer — solve the subproblems recursively, solving small enough ones directly; (3) Combine — merge the subproblem solutions into a solution of the original problem. Examples: Merge Sort, Quick Sort, binary search, Karatsuba multiplication, closest pair of points.
key_points: Three steps: divide, conquer (recursively), combine
Examples: Merge Sort, Quick Sort, Binary Search, Karatsuba

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: What is the backtracking technique?
reference_answer: Backtracking builds a solution step by step (e.g., choosing a value for each position); at each step it tries the possible choices in turn, and if a choice leads to a state violating constraints or that cannot become a solution, it 'backtracks' — undoing that choice and trying another. It is usually implemented recursively. Applications: N-Queens, Sudoku, generating permutations/combinations, maze path finding.
key_points: Builds solutions step by step, trying choices and undoing them at dead ends
Usually recursive; applications: N-Queens, Sudoku, combinatorial generation

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: What is the brute-force approach? When is it still a reasonable choice?
reference_answer: Brute force tries ALL possibilities to find a solution, e.g., checking every pair of elements to find two numbers summing to k (O(n²)). Pros: simple, easy to implement, guaranteed correct. Cons: usually high complexity (high-degree polynomial or exponential). It is still reasonable when the data is small, when a reference solution is needed to test a more optimized algorithm, or when no better algorithm is known.
key_points: Brute force tries everything: simple and correct but slow
Reasonable for small inputs or as a reference solution for testing

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Describe pre-order and post-order traversal of a binary tree, with one application of each.
reference_answer: Pre-order: visit the current node FIRST, then traverse the left subtree, then the right subtree (Root-Left-Right). Applications: copying a tree, serializing a tree structure (storing the root first to rebuild it), printing a directory structure. Post-order: traverse the left subtree, the right subtree, then visit the current node (Left-Right-Root). Applications: freeing/deleting a tree (children before parent), computing directory sizes (needing children's totals), evaluating expression trees.
key_points: Pre-order: Root-Left-Right, used to copy/serialize trees
Post-order: Left-Right-Root, used to delete trees and computations needing children's results first

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Depth and height of a node
question: Distinguish the depth and the height of a node in a tree.
reference_answer: The depth of a node is the number of edges on the path from the ROOT down to the node (the root has depth 0). The height of a node is the number of edges on the LONGEST path from the node down to a leaf (leaves have height 0). The height of the tree is the height of the root, which also equals the maximum depth in the tree. Depth is measured 'top-down', height 'bottom-up'.
key_points: Depth: edges from the root down to the node
Height: edges on the longest path from the node to a leaf; tree height = root height

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: General trees and the left-child right-sibling representation
question: How can a general tree (each node with an unbounded number of children) be represented using nodes with only two pointers?
reference_answer: Use the 'left-child, right-sibling' representation: each node has a pointer to its FIRST CHILD and a pointer to its NEXT SIBLING (the node with the same parent right after it). To traverse a node's children, go to the first child and then follow the chain of sibling pointers. This gives every node a fixed size regardless of its number of children and effectively turns a general tree into a binary tree.
key_points: Each node keeps pointers to its first child and next sibling
Nodes have a fixed size; a general tree is represented as a binary tree

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: What is a weighted graph? Give a real-world example.
reference_answer: A weighted graph is a graph where each edge is assigned a numeric value (weight) representing the cost, distance, time or capacity of that connection. Examples: a road map with cities as vertices, roads as edges and kilometers as weights; a computer network with latency as weights. Shortest path and minimum spanning tree problems operate on weighted graphs.
key_points: Each edge carries a weight such as distance, cost or time
The basis for shortest path and minimum spanning tree problems

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: What is a directed acyclic graph (DAG)? Give an application example.
reference_answer: A DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) is a directed graph with no cycles — you cannot start from a vertex, follow edge directions and return to it. DAGs naturally represent dependencies or orderings: course prerequisites, project tasks (task B starts only after A), software builds, Git commit history. A topological sort always exists for a DAG.
key_points: A DAG is a directed graph without cycles
Represents dependencies: prerequisites, project tasks, builds; always topologically sortable

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: What is the degree of a vertex? In a directed graph, how do in-degree and out-degree differ?
reference_answer: In an undirected graph, the degree of a vertex is the number of edges incident to it. The sum of all degrees equals twice the number of edges (each edge is counted at both ends). In a directed graph, in-degree is the number of edges coming INTO the vertex, and out-degree the number of edges going OUT. For example, on a one-way follow social network, in-degree is your number of followers and out-degree the number of people you follow.
key_points: Degree is the number of incident edges; total degree = 2 × edges in undirected graphs
Directed graphs: in-degree counts incoming edges, out-degree outgoing

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Distinguish the concepts of path, simple path and cycle in a graph.
reference_answer: A path is a sequence of vertices where consecutive vertices are connected by an edge. A simple path is a path that repeats no vertex. A cycle is a path whose first and last vertices coincide (with at least one edge; in undirected graphs usually requiring at least 3 distinct vertices and no repeated edges). The length of a path is the number of edges (or the total weight in weighted graphs).
key_points: Path: a sequence of vertices joined by edges; simple path: no repeated vertex
Cycle: a path returning to its starting vertex

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: When is an undirected graph connected?
reference_answer: An undirected graph is connected when there is at least one path between EVERY pair of vertices. If not connected, the graph consists of several connected components — each a maximal group of mutually connected vertices. Connectivity can be checked with one BFS/DFS from any vertex: the graph is connected if and only if the traversal visits every vertex.
key_points: Connected: every pair of vertices has a path
Check with one BFS/DFS visiting all vertices

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: A tree as a special graph
question: Why does a tree with n vertices always have exactly n - 1 edges?
reference_answer: A tree is a connected undirected graph with no cycles. Proof by induction: a 1-vertex tree has 0 edges; every tree with at least 2 vertices has a leaf (a vertex of degree 1); removing that leaf and its edge gives a tree with n - 1 vertices, which by the induction hypothesis has n - 2 edges, so the original tree has n - 1 edges. Consequences: adding any edge to a tree creates a cycle, removing any edge disconnects it.
key_points: A tree: connected, acyclic, always n - 1 edges
Adding an edge creates a cycle, removing one disconnects it

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Distinguish sparse and dense graphs. How does this affect the choice of representation?
reference_answer: A graph with V vertices can have up to about V² edges. A sparse graph has far fewer edges than V² (often E is around V, like road networks or social networks — each person knows a few hundred out of billions). A dense graph has E close to V². Sparse graphs should be represented with adjacency lists (O(V + E) memory); dense graphs can use an adjacency matrix (O(V²)) for O(1) edge checks.
key_points: Sparse: E much smaller than V²; dense: E close to V²
Sparse graphs use adjacency lists, dense graphs can use adjacency matrices

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: How does Shell Sort improve on Insertion Sort?
reference_answer: Insertion Sort is slow when elements are far from their correct positions because each move shifts them only one step. Shell Sort performs Insertion Sort on subsequences of elements a large gap apart, letting elements move far quickly; then it decreases the gap down to 1 (the last pass is ordinary Insertion Sort on a nearly sorted array). The complexity depends on the gap sequence and is usually much better than O(n²).
key_points: Insertion sort on elements a large gap apart, then shrinking the gap to 1
Lets elements move far quickly; performance depends on the gap sequence

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Describe the idea of Bucket Sort and the condition for it to be efficient.
reference_answer: Bucket Sort divides the value range into k equal 'buckets', distributes each element into the bucket corresponding to its value, sorts each bucket separately (often with Insertion Sort), then concatenates the buckets in order. It is efficient (near O(n) on average) when data is relatively UNIFORMLY distributed over a known range, e.g., real numbers in [0, 1). If data piles into a few buckets, performance degrades to that of the algorithm used inside the buckets.
key_points: Distribute elements into buckets by value, sort each bucket, then concatenate
Efficient when data is uniformly distributed over a known range

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Describe how to reverse an array in place and its complexity.
reference_answer: Use two indices: left starting at 0 and right at n - 1. While left < right: swap a[left] and a[right], then increment left and decrement right. Each symmetric pair is swapped exactly once. Time complexity O(n) (n/2 swaps), extra memory O(1) since only a few variables are used.
key_points: Two indices move from both ends toward the middle, swapping pairs
O(n) time, O(1) extra memory

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: What is a prefix sum array and which queries does it answer quickly?
reference_answer: A prefix sum array P is computed once with P[0] = 0 and P[i] = P[i-1] + a[i-1], i.e., P[i] is the sum of the first i elements. After O(n) preprocessing, the sum of any subarray a[l..r] is computed in O(1) as P[r+1] - P[l]. Very useful for many range-sum queries on an UNCHANGING array. It extends to 2D arrays to compute rectangle sums.
key_points: P[i] is the sum of the first i elements, O(n) preprocessing
Range sum [l, r] = P[r+1] - P[l] in O(1); suits static arrays

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: How does interpolation search differ from binary search in choosing the comparison position?
reference_answer: Binary search always compares with the MIDDLE element of the range. Interpolation search estimates the key's position from its value, like opening a dictionary near the end when looking for 'X': pos = lo + (key - a[lo]) × (hi - lo) / (a[hi] - a[lo]). For sorted arrays with uniformly distributed values, the average complexity is only O(log log n); but with skewed distributions the worst case degrades to O(n).
key_points: Estimates the position from the key's value instead of taking the midpoint
Average O(log log n) with uniform data, worst case O(n)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: How does Jump Search search a sorted array and what is its complexity?
reference_answer: Jump Search jumps through the array in blocks of size m (usually m = √n), checking the last element of each block until it finds a block whose last element is ≥ the key; then it searches linearly within that block. The total number of steps is about n/m + m, minimized when m = √n, so the complexity is O(√n) — slower than binary search but only moving forward (useful when moving backward is expensive, as on tape or skip-linked lists).
key_points: Jump in blocks of √n then search linearly within the block
O(√n); useful when moving backward is costly

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: The call stack and stack overflow
question: What role does the call stack play when executing recursive functions, and when does a stack overflow error occur?
reference_answer: Each function call pushes a 'frame' (stack frame) containing parameters, local variables and the return address onto the call stack; when the function ends, the frame is popped. With recursion, each level occupies a frame, so recursion depth n costs O(n) stack memory. The call stack has a limited size (usually a few MB); when recursion is too deep (missing base case, or large inputs such as recursively traversing a 1-million-element linked list), the stack fills up causing a stack overflow.
key_points: Each recursive call creates a stack frame; depth n costs O(n) memory
Stack overflow occurs with excessive depth or a missing base case

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: What is memoization and when does it speed up a recursive algorithm?
reference_answer: Memoization stores the results of function calls keyed by their input parameters (usually in a hash table or array); when the function is called again with the same parameters, the stored result is returned immediately instead of recomputing. It only helps when the recursive algorithm has OVERLAPPING SUBPROBLEMS (the same subproblem solved many times) and the function is pure (same input always gives the same result, no side effects).
key_points: Memoization stores results by parameters to avoid recomputation
Effective with overlapping subproblems and pure functions

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: What is Huffman coding used for and what greedy strategy is it based on?
reference_answer: Huffman coding is used for lossless data compression by assigning variable-length binary codes to characters: frequent characters get short codes, rare ones long codes; the codes are prefix codes (no code is a prefix of another), so decoding is unambiguous. Greedy strategy: repeatedly pick the two nodes with the SMALLEST frequencies (using a priority queue), merge them into a parent node whose frequency is their sum, until one tree remains; a character's code is the path from the root to its leaf (left 0, right 1).
key_points: Huffman compresses losslessly with frequency-based variable-length prefix codes
Greedy: repeatedly merge the two least frequent nodes using a priority queue

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Describe how to check whether a string is a palindrome using O(1) extra memory.
reference_answer: Use two pointers: i at the start and j at the end of the string. While i < j: if s[i] differs from s[j], conclude it is not a palindrome; otherwise increment i and decrement j. If the loop ends without finding a mismatched pair, the string is a palindrome. Complexity O(n) time and O(1) extra memory. If punctuation and case must be ignored, skip non-alphanumeric characters and compare after converting to lowercase.
key_points: Two pointers move inward from both ends comparing characters
O(n) time, O(1) memory; normalize if punctuation/case should be ignored

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Checking whether two strings are anagrams
question: How can you check whether two strings are anagrams of each other — containing the same characters with the same counts — in O(n) time?
reference_answer: Approach 1 (frequency counting): if the lengths differ they are not anagrams; use a count array (for small alphabets) or a hash table, incrementing for each character of the first string and decrementing for each character of the second; finally all counts must be 0. Complexity O(n). Approach 2: sort both strings and compare, simple but O(n log n).
key_points: Count character frequencies with an array/hash table, incrementing for one string and decrementing for the other
Counting is O(n); sorting and comparing is O(n log n)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Bit manipulation: checking powers of two
question: Why does the expression n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0 check whether n is a power of two?
reference_answer: A power of two has exactly ONE 1-bit in binary (e.g., 8 = 1000). Subtracting 1 turns that bit into 0 and all lower bits into 1 (7 = 0111). The AND of the two numbers is 0. For a number that is not a power of two (with two or more 1-bits), subtracting 1 only changes the bits from the lowest 1-bit downward, while higher 1-bits remain, so the AND is non-zero. The condition n > 0 excludes 0. The operation is O(1).
key_points: A power of two has exactly one 1-bit; n - 1 flips that bit and the lower bits
n & (n - 1) clears the lowest 1-bit; it is 0 only when there is a single 1-bit

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Finding the single element with XOR
question: Given an array where every element appears exactly twice except one that appears once, how do you find it in O(n) time and O(1) memory?
reference_answer: XOR all the elements of the array. XOR is commutative and associative, x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x. Therefore identical pairs cancel to 0 and the final result is the element that appears once. Only one accumulator variable is needed, so memory is O(1), and one pass gives O(n) time.
key_points: XOR all elements: identical pairs cancel to 0
The result is the single element; O(n) time, O(1) memory

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Euclid's algorithm for the greatest common divisor
question: Which property is Euclid's algorithm for the greatest common divisor (GCD) based on? What is its complexity?
reference_answer: It is based on gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b) for b ≠ 0, and gcd(a, 0) = a. Iterate (or recurse) until the second number becomes 0. Example: gcd(48, 18) = gcd(18, 12) = gcd(12, 6) = gcd(6, 0) = 6. The complexity is O(log(min(a, b))) because after every two steps the larger number at least halves.
key_points: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), stopping when the second number is 0
Complexity O(log min(a, b))

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Describe the Sieve of Eratosthenes for finding all primes up to n.
reference_answer: Create a marking array from 2 to n, initially treating everything as prime. For each number p from 2 onward still marked prime, cross out (mark as composite) all multiples of p starting from p² (smaller multiples were already crossed out by smaller primes). Only p up to √n needs to be considered. The numbers left unmarked are prime. Complexity O(n log log n), memory O(n).
key_points: Cross out multiples of each prime p starting from p², considering p up to √n
Complexity O(n log log n), memory O(n)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: How can a^n be computed in O(log n) multiplications instead of n?
reference_answer: Use fast exponentiation based on the binary representation of n: if n is even, a^n = (a^(n/2))²; if n is odd, a^n = a × a^(n-1). Iterative version: result = 1; while n > 0: if the lowest bit of n is 1, multiply result by a; square a; shift n right by one bit. Each step halves n, so only O(log n) multiplications are needed. It is often combined with taking a modulo at each step to avoid overflow when computing a^n mod m.
key_points: Based on the binary representation of the exponent: square, and multiply when the bit is 1
O(log n) multiplications; combine with modulo to avoid overflow

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: When a problem asks to output the result 'modulo 10^9 + 7', why should the modulo be taken at every step rather than only at the end?
reference_answer: Intermediate results (counts, factorials, powers) can far exceed the range of 64-bit integers, overflowing and producing wrong results. Thanks to (a + b) mod m = ((a mod m) + (b mod m)) mod m and (a × b) mod m = ((a mod m) × (b mod m)) mod m, we can take the modulo after each addition/multiplication to keep intermediate values below m without changing the final result. With m ≈ 10^9, the product of two numbers below m still fits in 64 bits.
key_points: Large intermediate values overflow integer types
Modular properties of addition/multiplication allow taking the modulo at each step without changing the result

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: How do you sort a list of students by score descending, and by name ascending for equal scores?
reference_answer: Use a lexicographic comparison over the tuple of criteria: compare scores first (reversed for descending); only when scores are equal compare names. Python example: sorted(students, key=lambda s: (-s.score, s.name)); Java: Comparator.comparing(Student::getScore).reversed().thenComparing(Student::getName). Alternatively, sort several times with a STABLE algorithm in reverse priority order: first by name, then by score.
key_points: Compare by a tuple of criteria in priority order (lexicographic)
Or apply stable sorts repeatedly from the secondary to the primary criterion

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Lower bound and upper bound variants
question: In a sorted array with duplicates, what are the lower bound and upper bound of a value x? Apply them to count occurrences of x.
reference_answer: The lower bound is the FIRST position with an element ≥ x; the upper bound is the first position with an element > x. Both can be found with binary search variants in O(log n). The number of occurrences of x equals upper_bound(x) - lower_bound(x). Example array [1, 2, 2, 2, 5], x = 2: lower bound = 1, upper bound = 4, occurrences = 3.
key_points: Lower bound: first position ≥ x; upper bound: first position > x
Occurrences = upper - lower, computed in O(log n)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: The loop condition in binary search
question: In a binary search implementation using lo = 0, hi = n - 1, why is the loop condition while (lo <= hi) rather than lo < hi, and why are the updates lo = mid + 1, hi = mid - 1?
reference_answer: With hi = n - 1, the search range is the CLOSED interval [lo, hi], so when lo = hi there is still one element to check — using lo < hi would skip it. Since a[mid] has already been compared and is not the answer, the next range excludes mid entirely: lo = mid + 1 or hi = mid - 1; writing lo = mid can loop forever when lo and hi are adjacent. General rule: choose an invariant (closed interval or half-open [lo, hi)) and keep both the stop condition and the updates consistent with it.
key_points: A closed interval [lo, hi] still has one element when lo = hi, so use lo <= hi
Exclude mid with mid ± 1 to avoid infinite loops; keep the invariant consistent

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Detecting duplicates with a hash set
question: How do you check whether an array contains duplicates in O(n) average time?
reference_answer: Traverse the array using a hash set of elements seen so far: for each element, if it is already in the set, there is a duplicate; otherwise add it. Each check/insert is O(1) on average, totaling O(n) time and O(n) memory. Compared with sorting and then comparing adjacent elements (O(n log n) time, possibly O(1) extra memory), the hash set is faster but uses more memory.
key_points: Traverse the array, checking and adding elements to a hash set
O(n) time, O(n) memory; a trade-off against sorting at O(n log n)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Finding the middle node with fast/slow pointers
question: How do you find the middle node of a singly linked list in a SINGLE pass?
reference_answer: Use two pointers starting at the head: the slow pointer moves 1 step at a time, the fast pointer 2 steps. When the fast pointer reaches the end of the list (or null), the slow pointer has traveled half the distance and is at the middle node. Complexity O(n) time, O(1) memory, without knowing the list length in advance.
key_points: The slow pointer moves 1 step, the fast pointer 2 steps
When the fast one reaches the end, the slow one is in the middle; one pass, O(1) memory

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Detecting a cycle in a linked list (Floyd)
question: How does Floyd's algorithm (tortoise and hare) detect whether a linked list has a cycle?
reference_answer: Use two pointers: the tortoise moves 1 step, the hare 2 steps each time. If the list has no cycle, the hare reaches null and stops. If there is a cycle, both eventually enter the loop; inside it, the distance between the hare and the tortoise decreases by 1 each step, so the hare is guaranteed to catch up with the tortoise. The algorithm is O(n) time, O(1) memory (instead of using a hash set of visited nodes costing O(n)).
key_points: The tortoise moves 1 step, the hare 2; without a cycle the hare reaches null
With a cycle the two pointers must meet; O(n) time, O(1) memory

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Describe the iterative algorithm for reversing a singly linked list.
reference_answer: Use three pointers: prev = null, curr = head. While curr is not null: save next = curr.next; reverse the link curr.next = prev; advance prev = curr, curr = next. When done, prev is the new head of the list. Saving next before reversing is mandatory, otherwise the rest of the list is lost. Complexity O(n) time, O(1) memory.
key_points: Use prev, curr, next; save next before reversing curr.next
At the end prev is the new head; O(n) time, O(1) memory

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Why do linked list operations (such as deleting elements or merging two lists) often use a dummy node placed before the head?
reference_answer: Many operations must handle special cases when changing the head itself (deleting the head, empty lists, inserting at the front). Placing a dummy node before the head gives EVERY real node a predecessor, so the same code works for every position, removing special-case branches and reducing bugs. The result returned is dummy.next. The cost is just one extra node.
key_points: A dummy node before the head gives every real node a predecessor
Removes special handling for the head/empty list; return dummy.next

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Distinguish linear and non-linear data structures, with examples of each.
reference_answer: Linear data structures arrange elements in a sequence, where each element (except the first and last) has exactly one predecessor and one successor, so all can be traversed in a single sequential pass: arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues. Non-linear structures organize elements hierarchically or as networks, where an element can be connected to several others: trees, heaps, graphs. Non-linear structures need dedicated traversal strategies such as DFS, BFS and tree traversal orders.
key_points: Linear: elements in sequence, each with one predecessor and one successor (arrays, lists, stacks, queues)
Non-linear: hierarchical or network relationships (trees, heaps, graphs), needing dedicated traversals

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Implementing a Queue with two Stacks
question: Describe how to implement a Queue with two Stacks and prove each operation has amortized O(1) cost.
reference_answer: Use an input stack (S_in) and an output stack (S_out). Enqueue: push onto S_in. Dequeue: if S_out is empty, pop every element from S_in and push it onto S_out (reversing the order, so the earliest element is now on top of S_out), then pop from S_out. A single dequeue may cost O(n) when transferring, but over its lifetime each element is pushed onto S_in once, moved to S_out once and popped from S_out once — at most about 4 basic operations. So the total cost of m operations is O(m), i.e., amortized O(1) per operation.
key_points: Enqueue onto S_in; dequeue from S_out, transferring all of S_in only when S_out is empty
Each element moves a constant number of times, so the amortized cost is O(1)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Design a Stack supporting push, pop, top and getMin all in O(1).
reference_answer: Use an auxiliary stack (minStack) in parallel: when pushing x, push x onto the main stack and push min(x, top of minStack) onto minStack (or only push when x ≤ top of minStack to save space). When popping, pop from both stacks (or pop minStack only when the removed element equals its top). getMin returns the top of minStack. Key idea: at each stack state, the minimum of the elements below is fixed until they are popped, so it can be recorded at push time.
key_points: Use an auxiliary stack storing the minimum at each level of the main stack
Push/pop both in sync, getMin reads the auxiliary top — all O(1)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: How is a monotonic stack used to find the 'next greater element' for each element of an array in O(n)?
reference_answer: Traverse the array from left to right, maintaining a stack of indices of elements that have NOT yet found their next greater element, with values decreasing from bottom to top. For the current element a[i]: while the stack is non-empty and a[top] < a[i], a[i] is the next greater element of top — record it and pop. Then push i. Indices left in the stack at the end have no greater element (assign -1). Each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the total is O(n) instead of O(n²) with two nested loops.
key_points: The stack keeps unanswered indices with decreasing values
A new element pops all smaller ones and is their answer; each index pushed/popped once gives O(n)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Sliding window maximum with a deque
question: Given an array of n elements and a window of length k, find the maximum of each window in O(n) using a deque.
reference_answer: Maintain a deque of INDICES of elements that could be the maximum of the current or a future window, with values decreasing from front to back. For each i: (1) remove from the front indices that have left the window (≤ i - k); (2) remove from the back indices with values ≤ a[i] — they can never be the maximum because a[i] is larger and lasts longer; (3) append i; (4) when i ≥ k - 1, the window maximum is a[front of deque]. Each index enters and leaves the deque at most once, so the total is O(n), compared with O(n·k) when recomputing the max for each window.
key_points: The deque keeps indices with decreasing values, dropping expired ones at the front and smaller ones at the back
The front is always the window maximum; each index enters/leaves once, O(n)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Why does building a heap from an array of n elements with 'bottom-up heapify' cost only O(n), while inserting n elements one by one costs O(n log n)?
reference_answer: Bottom-up: call sift-down for nodes from the last internal node (index n/2 - 1) back to the root. The cost of sift-down for a node is proportional to its HEIGHT (distance down to the leaves), not its depth. In a complete tree, about n/2 nodes are leaves (cost 0), n/4 have height 1, n/8 height 2... The total cost ≈ n × Σ h/2^(h+1), a series converging to a constant, so the total is O(n). In contrast, inserting one by one uses sift-up, whose cost is proportional to DEPTH; most nodes are at deep levels (about log n), so the total can reach O(n log n).
key_points: Bottom-up uses sift-down, costing by node height; most nodes have small height
The total Σ n·h/2^(h+1) = O(n); repeated insertion uses sift-up by depth, O(n log n)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Finding the k largest elements with a size-k heap
question: Given a very large data stream (not fitting in memory), how do you find the k largest elements? Analyze the complexity.
reference_answer: Maintain a MIN-heap of size at most k. For each element x in the stream: if the heap has fewer than k elements, add it; if full and x is larger than the heap's root (the smallest of the current k largest), replace the root with x and sift down. At the end, the heap contains the k largest elements. Complexity O(n log k) time and O(k) memory — much better than sorting everything at O(n log n) and O(n) memory when k is small. Common confusion: finding the k LARGEST uses a MIN-heap, because we need to quickly evict the smallest of the group.
key_points: Maintain a min-heap of k elements, replacing the root when a larger element arrives
O(n log k) time, O(k) memory; suited for large streams

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Median of a data stream with two heaps
question: Design a structure supporting adding numbers and querying the current median efficiently.
reference_answer: Use two heaps: a 'low' MAX-heap holding the smaller half and a 'high' MIN-heap holding the larger half, with invariants: every element of 'low' ≤ every element of 'high', and their sizes differ by at most 1. Adding x: put it into 'low' if x ≤ top of 'low', otherwise into 'high'; then rebalance by moving the top of the larger heap to the other if the difference exceeds 1. The median is the top of the larger heap (odd count) or the average of both tops (even count). Adding is O(log n), querying O(1).
key_points: A max-heap holds the smaller half, a min-heap the larger half, sizes differing by at most 1
Insert O(log n); the median is read from the heap tops in O(1)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Design an LRU (Least Recently Used) cache of fixed capacity supporting get and put in O(1).
reference_answer: Combine two structures: (1) a hash table mapping key → node in a list, to find elements in O(1); (2) a DOUBLY linked list keeping usage order: the head is the most recently used, the tail the least recently used. get(k): look up the hash table; if present, detach the node and move it to the head (O(1) thanks to prev/next pointers), returning the value. put(k, v): if present, update and move to the head; if absent and the cache is full, remove the tail node (also deleting its key from the hash table), then insert the new node at the head. The doubly linked list is needed to remove an arbitrary node in O(1). Java provides LinkedHashMap with accessOrder = true.
key_points: Hash table for O(1) lookup + doubly linked list for usage order
get/put move nodes to the head, evict the tail when full; the doubly linked list allows O(1) removal

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Binary search on the answer space
question: There are n piles of bananas and h hours; each hour a monkey eats at most v bananas from one pile (if a pile has fewer than v, it eats the whole pile and rests the rest of the hour). Find the minimum speed v to finish within h hours. Explain why binary search applies.
reference_answer: Instead of searching an array, binary search over the ANSWER SPACE v ∈ [1, max(pile)]. The key condition is MONOTONICITY: if speed v finishes in time, every larger speed does too; the hours needed at speed v are Σ ⌈pile_i / v⌉, computed in O(n). Find the smallest feasible v: if v finishes in time, narrow to the left half (keeping v), otherwise go right. Complexity O(n log M) with M the largest pile. This technique applies to many 'find the minimum/maximum value satisfying a condition' problems as long as the check function is monotonic.
key_points: Binary search over the range of answer values instead of an array
Requires a monotonic check function; complexity O(n log M)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: A sorted ascending array has been rotated at an unknown position (e.g., [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]), with distinct elements. How do you search for a value in O(log n)?
reference_answer: A binary search variant: at each step with mid, at least ONE of the halves [lo, mid] or [mid, hi] is guaranteed sorted. If a[lo] ≤ a[mid], the left half is sorted: if a[lo] ≤ x < a[mid], search left, otherwise right. Otherwise the right half is sorted: if a[mid] < x ≤ a[hi], search right, otherwise left. Each step eliminates half, so O(log n). With duplicates (a[lo] = a[mid] = a[hi]) we cannot tell which half is sorted, and the worst case degrades to O(n).
key_points: At each step one half is guaranteed sorted; check whether x lies in that half
O(log n) for distinct elements; with duplicates the worst case is O(n)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Merge k sorted lists (N elements in total) into one sorted list. Compare merging pairs one after another with using a min-heap.
reference_answer: Sequential merging (list 1 with 2, the result with 3, ...): the result list keeps growing, costing O(N·k) in total when lists have similar lengths. Using a min-heap: insert the first element of each list into a heap of size k; repeatedly extract the smallest, append it to the result, and insert the next element from the same list. Each element enters/leaves the heap once at O(log k), totaling O(N log k). Pairwise divide-and-conquer merging (like Merge Sort over the lists) also achieves O(N log k). This is the basis of k-way merge in external sorting.
key_points: Sequential merging costs O(N·k)
A k-element min-heap or divide-and-conquer merging achieves O(N log k); basis of k-way merge

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: The number of inversions of an array is the number of pairs (i, j) with i < j and a[i] > a[j]. How can it be counted in O(n log n) instead of O(n²)?
reference_answer: Embed counting into Merge Sort. Inversions = inversions within the left half + within the right half + 'cross' inversions (one element in each half). The halves are counted recursively and are then sorted. During the merge, when an element is taken from the RIGHT half (because it is smaller than the current a[i] of the left half), it is smaller than all remaining elements of the left half (from i to the end, since it is sorted), so add (remaining count in the left half) inversions. The counting cost blends into the O(n) merge step, totaling O(n log n). The inversion count measures 'unsortedness' and equals the number of swaps performed by Bubble Sort.
key_points: Total = inversions in each half + cross inversions, counted during Merge Sort's merge
When taking from the right half, add the number of remaining left elements; total O(n log n)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: State the Master Theorem for the recurrence T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n) and apply it to Merge Sort and binary search.
reference_answer: Compare f(n) with n^(log_b a) (the cost of the leaves in the recursion tree): (1) If f(n) = O(n^(log_b a - ε)) — cost concentrated at the leaves — then T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)). (2) If f(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)) — equal cost per level — then T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) · log n). (3) If f(n) = Ω(n^(log_b a + ε)) and the regularity condition holds — cost concentrated at the root — then T(n) = Θ(f(n)). Merge Sort: a = 2, b = 2, f(n) = n = n^(log_2 2) → case 2, Θ(n log n). Binary search: a = 1, b = 2, f(n) = 1 = n^0 → case 2, Θ(log n).
key_points: Compare f(n) with n^(log_b a): leaves dominate, balanced, or root dominates
Merge Sort Θ(n log n) and Binary Search Θ(log n) both fall under case 2

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: How does Karatsuba's algorithm multiply two n-digit numbers faster than the O(n²) schoolbook method?
reference_answer: Split each number into two halves: x = a·10^m + b, y = c·10^m + d. The product xy = ac·10^(2m) + (ad + bc)·10^m + bd normally needs 4 half-size multiplications, giving T(n) = 4T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n²) — no improvement. Karatsuba observes that ad + bc = (a + b)(c + d) - ac - bd, so only 3 multiplications are needed: ac, bd and (a + b)(c + d). The recurrence T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n) gives O(n^(log_2 3)) ≈ O(n^1.585). For very large numbers (cryptography, high-precision arithmetic) the improvement is significant; for small numbers overhead makes schoolbook faster, so practical implementations use a cutoff threshold.
key_points: Use (a + b)(c + d) - ac - bd to reduce 4 sub-multiplications to 3
T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n^1.585); use a cutoff to schoolbook for small numbers

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Closest pair of points by divide and conquer
question: Describe the divide-and-conquer algorithm for finding the closest pair among n points in the plane in O(n log n).
reference_answer: Sort the points by x, split them in half with a vertical line, recursively find the minimum distances d_left and d_right in the two halves, and set d = min. A closest 'cross' pair (one point in each half) can only lie within a strip of width 2d around the dividing line. Sort the points in the strip by y; each point only needs to be compared with a constant number of following points (at most about 7) because a d × 2d rectangle can only hold a constant number of points pairwise at distance ≥ d. The combine step is O(n) (if a y-sorted list is maintained), so T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n), compared with O(n²) when checking every pair.
key_points: Split by x, solve both halves, only examine the strip of width 2d around the line
Each strip point is compared with a constant number of following points by y; total O(n log n)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Backtracking and pruning in the N-Queens problem
question: In the N-Queens problem, how do you check for conflicts in O(1) when placing each queen, and how does pruning reduce the search space?
reference_answer: Place exactly one queen per row, starting from row 0. Use three boolean arrays marking: occupied columns, main diagonals (identified by row - column, offset by n - 1 to be non-negative) and anti-diagonals (row + column). Placing a queen at (r, c) is valid when all three marks are free — an O(1) check; when backtracking, unmark them. Pruning: as soon as a position conflicts, the whole subtree below it is skipped, so the number of states actually explored is far smaller than brute-forcing n^n placements or n! permutations. Further optimizations use bitmasks and symmetry.
key_points: One queen per row; arrays marking columns, (r - c) diagonals and (r + c) diagonals give O(1) checks
Pruning on conflicts removes entire subtrees, far smaller than brute force

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: How do you generate all 2^n subsets of an n-element set using bitmasks? When is this approach no longer suitable?
reference_answer: Each integer mask from 0 to 2^n - 1 represents a subset: bit i equal to 1 means element i is in the subset. Loop mask from 0 to 2^n - 1 and, for each mask, scan n bits to collect the elements. Total cost O(n·2^n). Pros: simple, non-recursive, easy to use as the state for Bitmask DP. Limitations: the number of subsets grows exponentially, so it is only feasible for small n (about n ≤ 20 - 25), and it is limited by the number of bits in the integer type; larger n requires exploiting problem structure (DP, meet-in-the-middle, pruning).
key_points: Each mask 0..2^n - 1 corresponds to a subset; bit i says whether element i is included
Cost O(n·2^n), feasible only for small n

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Describe the algorithm for finding the next lexicographic permutation (next permutation) of a sequence, e.g., [1, 3, 5, 4, 2].
reference_answer: (1) From right to left, find the first position i with a[i] < a[i+1] (in the example, i points to 3, since [5, 4, 2] is decreasing). If none exists, the sequence is the largest permutation. (2) From right to left, find the first j with a[j] > a[i] (element 4). (3) Swap a[i] and a[j] → [1, 4, 5, 3, 2]. (4) Reverse the suffix after position i (which is decreasing) to make it increasing → [1, 4, 2, 3, 5]. Complexity O(n) per call, O(1) memory, correctly handling duplicates. Repeating from the ascending sorted sequence generates all permutations in lexicographic order.
key_points: Find the last i with a[i] < a[i+1], the last j with a[j] > a[i], and swap
Reverse the suffix after i; O(n) per call, handles duplicates

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Describe Kahn's algorithm (in-degree based) for topological sorting, and how it also detects whether the graph has a cycle.
reference_answer: Compute every vertex's in-degree; put all vertices with in-degree 0 (depending on nobody) into a queue. Repeat: take a vertex u out, append it to the result; for each edge u → v, decrement v's in-degree, and if it reaches 0 enqueue v. Complexity O(V + E). If at the end the result has fewer than V vertices, the remaining vertices all have permanently positive in-degree — they lie on (or depend on) a cycle, so the graph is not a DAG. Replacing the queue with a min-heap yields the lexicographically smallest topological order.
key_points: Repeatedly take in-degree-0 vertices and decrement neighbors' in-degrees; O(V + E)
Fewer than V vertices in the result means a cycle; a min-heap gives the lexicographically smallest order

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Basic Dijkstra only gives shortest distances. How do you print the actual shortest path from source s to target t?
reference_answer: Maintain an additional predecessor array prev[]: whenever an edge u → v reduces the distance (dist[u] + w < dist[v]), besides updating dist[v], set prev[v] = u. After the algorithm finishes, walk back from t following prev[] to s and reverse the resulting sequence to get the path from s to t. If dist[t] is still infinity, there is no path. The prev[] pointers of all vertices form the 'shortest path tree' rooted at s. The extra cost is O(V) memory and O(path length) for reconstruction.
key_points: Store prev[v] = u whenever edge u → v improves dist[v]
Walk back from t through prev[] and reverse; the pointers form the shortest path tree

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: For a graph whose edge weights are only 0 or 1, how do you find shortest paths in O(V + E) instead of Dijkstra's O((V + E) log V)?
reference_answer: Use 0-1 BFS with a double-ended queue (deque): when examining an edge u → v with weight w and dist[u] + w < dist[v], update dist[v]; if w = 0 push v to the FRONT of the deque (same distance level as u), if w = 1 push it to the BACK. This keeps the deque holding vertices with non-decreasing distances differing by at most 1, so it acts as a priority queue without a heap. A vertex may be pushed several times but the total cost is O(V + E). Applications: grids where going straight costs 0 and turning costs 1; minimum number of direction changes/walls to break.
key_points: Weight-0 edges push to the front of the deque, weight-1 edges to the back
The deque acts as a priority queue; total O(V + E)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: In a grid with many hospitals, compute each cell's distance to the NEAREST hospital. Why is running BFS separately from each hospital inefficient, and how does multi-source BFS solve it?
reference_answer: Running a separate BFS for each of k hospitals costs O(k·N) where N is the number of cells. Multi-source BFS puts ALL hospitals into the initial queue with distance 0, then runs a normal BFS once. This is equivalent to adding a virtual 'super source' connected to every hospital with weight-0 edges. Since BFS expands layer by layer, the first time a cell is visited gives its distance to the nearest hospital. Total cost O(N). Applications: spreading processes (rotting oranges), distance to the nearest obstacle.
key_points: Put all sources into the initial queue with distance 0 and run BFS once
Equivalent to adding a virtual super source; O(N) instead of O(k·N)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Counting islands in a grid (flood fill)
question: Given an m × n grid of land (1) and water (0), count the islands (land cells connected in 4 directions). Describe the algorithm and implementation caveats.
reference_answer: Treat the grid as an implicit graph: each cell is a vertex connected to its 4 neighbors. Scan every cell; when encountering an unvisited land cell, increment the island counter and run DFS/BFS (flood fill) from it to mark all connected land cells as visited. The number of times a flood fill starts equals the number of connected components = the number of islands. Complexity O(m·n). Caveats: check bounds before accessing neighbors; mark cells as visited when pushing them into the queue/stack; for large grids (e.g., 2000 × 2000) recursive DFS can overflow the stack, so use BFS or DFS with an explicit stack; marking directly in the grid is possible if modifying the input is allowed.
key_points: Each unvisited land cell found starts a flood fill marking the whole island and increments the counter
O(m·n); check bounds, mark on push, avoid deep recursion on large grids

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Shortest paths on a DAG via topological order
question: Why can shortest paths from one source on a directed acyclic graph (DAG) be found in O(V + E), even with negative weights?
reference_answer: Topologically sort the vertices, then process them in that order and 'relax' all outgoing edges of each vertex. Since every edge goes forward in topological order, when processing vertex u all paths into u have already been considered (all vertices before u are finished), so dist[u] is final. Each edge is relaxed exactly once, so O(V + E). There is no non-negative weight requirement as in Dijkstra because there are no cycles. Negating weights (or switching min to max) finds the LONGEST path on a DAG — NP-hard on general graphs but easy on DAGs, used in project scheduling (the critical path).
key_points: Process in topological order and relax edges, each edge once, O(V + E)
No non-negative weight requirement; switching to max finds the longest path (critical path)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Cheapest path with at most K edges
question: Find the cheapest flight route from city A to B with at most K stops. Why does ordinary Dijkstra not solve this correctly, and how does Bellman-Ford with a bounded number of rounds work?
reference_answer: Dijkstra optimizes cost while ignoring the number of edges; once a vertex is 'settled' with the minimum cost, that cost may use too many hops, while a more expensive route with fewer hops is the one satisfying the constraint — Dijkstra discards it. Bounded Bellman-Ford: after round i, dist[v] is the minimum cost using at most i edges. Run exactly K + 1 rounds (K stops = K + 1 flights), and in each round relax using a COPY of the previous round's dist — updating in place lets one round relax several consecutive edges and exceed the edge limit. Complexity O(K·E). Alternative: Dijkstra/BFS over states (vertex, edges used).
key_points: Dijkstra ignores the edge-count constraint and may discard valid routes
Bellman-Ford for K + 1 rounds, each using a copy of the previous dist; O(K·E)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Two Sum with a hash table
question: Given an unsorted array and a target T, find two indices whose values sum to T in O(n). Compare with the two-pointer approach.
reference_answer: Traverse the array once with a hash table mapping value → index of elements seen so far. For each a[i], check whether T - a[i] is in the table; if so, return the pair of indices, otherwise add a[i] to the table. Checking before inserting avoids pairing an element with itself. Complexity O(n) average time, O(n) memory. The two-pointer approach requires a sorted array: if sorting is needed first it costs O(n log n) and loses the original indices (which must be stored alongside), but uses O(1) extra memory if the array is already sorted.
key_points: One pass, looking up T - a[i] among seen elements before inserting a[i]
O(n) time and memory; two pointers need a sorted array, O(1) memory

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Kadane's algorithm for maximum subarray sum
question: Describe Kadane's algorithm for the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray in O(n), and explain it from a dynamic programming perspective.
reference_answer: Let best_end[i] be the maximum sum of a subarray ENDING at i. That subarray is either just a[i], or the best subarray ending at i - 1 extended by a[i]: best_end[i] = max(a[i], best_end[i-1] + a[i]). Meaning: if the accumulated sum so far is negative, drop it and restart from a[i]. The answer is the max of all best_end[i]. Since each step only needs the previous value, two variables suffice: O(1) memory, O(n) time. Note the all-negative case: initialize with a[0] (not 0) to return the largest element rather than an empty subarray.
key_points: best_end[i] = max(a[i], best_end[i-1] + a[i]); the answer is the max over all best_end
O(n) time, O(1) memory; initialize with a[0] to handle all-negative arrays

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Given the money in houses arranged in a row, you cannot take from two adjacent houses; find the maximum total. Write the DP formula and extend it to houses arranged in a circle.
reference_answer: dp[i] = maximum total considering the first i houses. For house i there are two choices: skip it (dp[i-1]) or take it (dp[i-2] + a[i]), so dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + a[i]), with dp[0] = 0, dp[1] = a[1]. Only two variables are needed: O(n) time, O(1) memory. When houses form a circle, the first and last become adjacent, so both cannot be taken: solve two linear problems — excluding the last house (houses 1..n-1) and excluding the first (houses 2..n) — and take the larger result.
key_points: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + a[i]), O(n) time, O(1) memory
Circular version: solve twice excluding the first or the last house and take the max

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Jump Game with a greedy approach
question: Given an array a where a[i] is the maximum jump length from position i, check whether the last position is reachable from position 0 in O(n), and explain why greedy is correct.
reference_answer: Maintain reach = the farthest reachable position. Iterate i from 0: if i > reach, position i is unreachable, so stop and return false; otherwise update reach = max(reach, i + a[i]); if reach ≥ n - 1 return true. Correctness: the set of reachable positions is always a contiguous range [0, reach] — if position j is reachable, every position before j is too (by jumping shorter), so tracking only the right boundary suffices. There is no need to try every jump combination as DP/brute force does (O(n²) or worse).
key_points: Track the farthest reachable position and stop when i exceeds it
Correct because reachable positions form a contiguous range; O(n) instead of O(n²) DP

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Given a list of intervals [start, end], merge all overlapping intervals. Describe the algorithm and its complexity.
reference_answer: Sort the intervals by start. Traverse them while maintaining the current merged interval: if the next interval's start ≤ the current interval's end, they overlap, so update end = max(both ends) — max is required because a later interval may lie entirely within the previous one; otherwise push the current interval to the result and start a new one. After sorting, comparing only with the last interval in the result suffices because all earlier ones end sooner. Complexity O(n log n) due to sorting; the merging pass is O(n).
key_points: Sort by start, merge when start ≤ current end
New end = max of both ends; total O(n log n)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Given meetings with start and end times, find the minimum number of meeting rooms needed. Present two solutions.
reference_answer: Approach 1 (min-heap): sort meetings by start time; keep a min-heap of the end times of rooms in use. For each meeting, if the earliest-ending room (heap top) is free before the start time, reuse it (pop), then push the new end time. The largest heap size is the answer. Approach 2 (sweep line): split into events (time, +1 at start, -1 at end), sort by time (end events before start events at the same time, since the room is freed in time), sweep and track the maximum number of simultaneous meetings. Both are O(n log n). The answer is the maximum number of overlapping intervals at any instant.
key_points: Min-heap of end times: reuse the earliest-free room; the largest heap size is the answer
Sweep line: +1/-1 events, ends before starts at ties; both O(n log n)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: You must perform m operations 'add v to every element from l to r' on an n-element array and then print the resulting array. How can you achieve O(n + m) instead of O(n·m)?
reference_answer: Use a difference array d with d[i] = a[i] - a[i-1]. Adding v to range [l, r] only changes two positions of the difference array: d[l] += v and d[r+1] -= v — O(1) per operation. After m operations, rebuild the array by taking prefix sums of d: a[i] = a[i-1] + d[i], costing O(n). Total O(n + m). This is the inverse of the prefix sum array. Limitation: it only fits when all updates happen before queries; if updates and queries interleave, a Fenwick tree or segment tree is needed.
key_points: Add to range [l, r] via d[l] += v, d[r+1] -= v in O(1)
Rebuild with prefix sums O(n); suits updates-then-queries only

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: How does the recurrence of the unbounded knapsack (each item type can be taken any number of times) differ from 0/1 Knapsack?
reference_answer: 0/1 Knapsack: dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-1][w - w_i] + v_i) — if item i is taken, move to the subproblem of the items BEFORE i (each item is used once). Unbounded: dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i][w - w_i] + v_i) — if item i is taken, stay in row i, allowing item i to be taken again. With a one-dimensional array dp[w] = best value with capacity w, the compact form is dp[w] = max over all items i with w_i ≤ w of dp[w - w_i] + v_i. Complexity O(n·W) (pseudo-polynomial). Applications: rod cutting, coin change with unlimited coins.
key_points: Unbounded stays in row i when taking item i (dp[i][w - w_i]), while 0/1 moves to row i - 1
One-dimensional form dp[w] = max(dp[w - w_i] + v_i); O(n·W)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Partitioning an array into two equal-sum subsets
question: Check whether an array of positive integers can be split into two subsets with equal sums. What problem does it reduce to, and what is the complexity?
reference_answer: If the total S is odd it is impossible. If S is even, the problem is equivalent to: does a subset sum to exactly S/2 (Subset Sum) — a form of 0/1 Knapsack. Use a boolean array can[t] = whether sum t is achievable; initialize can[0] = true; for each element x, iterate t DECREASING from S/2 down to x and set can[t] = can[t] or can[t - x] (decreasing so each element is used only once). The answer is can[S/2]. Complexity O(n·S) time, O(S) memory — pseudo-polynomial, efficient when the total is not too large. It can be sped up with a bitset: bits |= bits << x.
key_points: Reduce to Subset Sum with target S/2 (impossible if S is odd)
Boolean DP iterating t downward per element, O(n·S); optimizable with a bitset

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Find the length of the longest palindromic subsequence (not necessarily contiguous) of a string s. Write the DP formula and state its relation to LCS.
reference_answer: Let dp[i][j] be the length of the longest palindromic subsequence within s[i..j]. If s[i] = s[j], dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j-1] + 2 (the two end characters surround an inner palindrome); otherwise dp[i][j] = max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Base case dp[i][i] = 1. Compute by increasing interval length (or i decreasing, j increasing). Complexity O(n²) time and memory (memory reducible to O(n)). Relation: the answer equals LCS(s, reverse of s). This differs from the longest CONTIGUOUS palindromic substring problem, which has an O(n) solution (Manacher).
key_points: dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j-1] + 2 if s[i] = s[j], otherwise max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1])
O(n²); equals the LCS of s and its reverse

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: Given a string s and a dictionary, check whether s can be segmented into a sequence of dictionary words. Write the DP formula and analyze the complexity.
reference_answer: Let ok[i] = true if the prefix s[0..i) can be segmented. ok[0] = true. ok[i] = true if there exists j < i with ok[j] = true and s[j..i) in the dictionary. The answer is ok[n]. With the dictionary in a hash set, there are O(n²) pairs (j, i), and creating/hashing each substring costs O(length), about O(n³) in the worst case; optimize by only considering j with i - j not exceeding the longest word length L, giving O(n·L²), or use a Trie to walk from position j and find all matching words in one pass. Plain recursion without memoization can blow up exponentially on strings like 'aaaa...ab'.
key_points: ok[i] = exists j with ok[j] and s[j..i) in the dictionary
Limit word length or use a Trie to optimize; unmemoized recursion can be exponential

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Counting coin change ways: combinations vs permutations
question: Count the number of ways to make amount S from given denominations (unlimited quantities). Why does the order of the two loops (denominations outer vs amount outer) give two different answers?
reference_answer: Use ways[0] = 1. Approach A — outer loop over DENOMINATIONS, inner loop over amounts t increasing: ways[t] += ways[t - c]. Each denomination is 'introduced' in a fixed order, so each multiset of coins is counted exactly once — counting COMBINATIONS (1+2 and 2+1 are the same way). Approach B — outer loop over AMOUNTS, inner loop over denominations: ways[t] = Σ ways[t - c] — at each amount the last coin can be any denomination, so different orders are counted separately — counting PERMUTATIONS/ordered sequences (1+2 differs from 2+1), like the climbing-stairs problem. Both are O(n·S). Determine which one the problem asks for; take a modulo if results are large.
key_points: Denominations in the outer loop: counts combinations (order-independent)
Amount in the outer loop: counts ordered sequences; both O(n·S)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Catalan numbers and counting distinct BSTs
question: How many structurally distinct binary search trees contain the keys 1..n? Derive the recurrence.
reference_answer: Let G(n) be the number of distinct BSTs with n keys. Choosing key i as the root: the left subtree contains the i - 1 smaller keys, the right subtree the n - i larger keys; the subtrees are independent, giving G(i-1) × G(n-i) ways. Summing over all root choices: G(n) = Σ_{i=1..n} G(i-1)·G(n-i), with G(0) = G(1) = 1. This is the Catalan sequence: 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42..., with closed form C(n) = (2n)! / ((n+1)!·n!), growing roughly like 4^n / n^1.5. Computing via DP takes O(n²). Catalan numbers also count valid parenthesizations, lattice paths not crossing the diagonal, and triangulations of polygons.
key_points: Choosing root i: G(n) = Σ G(i-1)·G(n-i), G(0) = 1
These are Catalan numbers (2n)!/((n+1)!·n!); they also count valid parentheses and polygon triangulations

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Validating a BST and a common mistake
question: A BST validation solution only compares each node with its direct left and right children (left < node < right). Why is it wrong? Give the correct approach.
reference_answer: The BST property is global: EVERY node in the left subtree must be smaller than the root, not just the direct child. Counterexample: root 10, left child 5, right child of 5 is 15 — every parent-child pair looks 'correct' but 15 lies in the left subtree of 10, violating the property. Correct approach 1: recursively pass a valid range (min, max) to each node; going left updates max = node value, going right updates min = node value; a node outside its range means not a BST. Correct approach 2: in-order traversal checking that values are strictly increasing (only remembering the previous value). Both are O(n). Use sufficiently wide (or null) initial bounds so boundary values of the integer type do not break it.
key_points: Comparing only parent-child pairs misses violations by deeper descendants
Pass a (min, max) range recursively or check strictly increasing in-order; O(n)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Lowest common ancestor (LCA) in a BST
question: How do you find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes p, q in a binary search tree in O(h)?
reference_answer: Exploit BST ordering: start from the root; if both p and q are smaller than the current node, the LCA is in the left subtree, so go left; if both are larger, go right; otherwise (p and q are on different sides, or one of them is the current node) the current node is the LCA — the first 'split point' of the two root paths. Complexity O(h) where h is the tree height, O(log n) for balanced trees, O(1) memory iteratively. For a general binary tree (no ordering), a recursive traversal of the whole tree in O(n) is needed.
key_points: From the root: both smaller go left, both larger go right
The first split point is the LCA; O(h), general trees need O(n)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: The diameter of a binary tree is the length of the longest path between any two nodes. How do you compute it in O(n)?
reference_answer: The longest path passes through some 'highest' node u, with length equal to the height of u's left subtree plus the height of its right subtree (in edges, including the edges to u). Use a post-order traversal: the recursive function returns a node's height; at each node, sum the heights of both branches to update a global answer, then return 1 + max(both heights) to the parent. Each node is processed once, so O(n). Common mistake: assuming the diameter always passes through the root. For general trees (as graphs), another method: BFS from any vertex to find the farthest vertex a, then BFS from a to find the farthest vertex b; the a-b distance is the diameter.
key_points: At each node, the path through it = left height + right height; update the answer in post-order
O(n); the diameter need not pass through the root; general trees can use two BFS passes

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Serializing and deserializing a binary tree
question: How do you serialize a binary tree to a string and restore it exactly? Why is an in-order sequence alone not enough?
reference_answer: A single traversal sequence (in-order or pre-order) does not uniquely determine the tree: many differently shaped trees produce the same in-order sequence (e.g., left-leaning and right-leaning trees with the same keys). A common approach: pre-order traversal recording NULL children with a special marker, e.g., '1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,#'. To restore, read sequentially: '#' returns null, otherwise create a node and recursively build its left and right subtrees. Both directions are O(n). Alternatives: store pre-order + in-order sequences (with distinct keys), or level-order (BFS) with nulls. For a BST, the pre-order sequence alone suffices because key order determines the structure.
key_points: A traversal without null markers does not uniquely determine a tree
Pre-order with null markers, read sequentially to rebuild, O(n); BSTs need only pre-order

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
question: A binary tree is height-balanced if at every node the heights of the two subtrees differ by at most 1. Why does computing heights separately at each node cost O(n²) for skewed trees, and what is the optimal approach?
reference_answer: Naive approach: at each node call height(left) and height(right), each traversing the whole subtree; for a skewed tree (like a list), the total cost is n + (n-1) + ... = O(n²). Optimal approach: a single post-order traversal where the function returns the node's height, or a special value -1 if the subtree is already unbalanced. At each node: get the left and right heights (if either is -1, return -1 immediately — early exit), if the difference > 1 return -1, otherwise return 1 + max. Each node is visited once, so O(n). This is a general pattern: combine computing information and checking it in the same bottom-up traversal.
key_points: Computing heights separately at each node repeats work, O(n²) for skewed trees
Post-order returning the height or -1 when unbalanced, with early exit; O(n)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Augmenting trees with subtree sizes (Order Statistic Tree)
question: How do you augment a balanced BST to find the k-th smallest element and compute the rank of a value in O(log n)?
reference_answer: Store at each node an extra field size = number of nodes in its subtree (size = size(left) + size(right) + 1). Finding the k-th element: at node x with t = size(left): if k = t + 1, x is the answer; if k ≤ t, find the k-th in the left subtree; otherwise find the (k - t - 1)-th in the right subtree. Computing the rank of value v: walk down from the root, adding size(left) + 1 of each node passed whenever going right. Both are O(h) = O(log n) on balanced trees. Requirement: size must be maintained correctly on insertion, deletion and also during rebalancing rotations (affecting only a constant number of nodes).
key_points: Each node stores its subtree size, updated on insert/delete/rotation
Find the k-th element and compute ranks by descending based on the left subtree size, O(log n)

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Deletion in Open Addressing and tombstones
question: In a hash table using Open Addressing (linear probing), why can't an element be deleted by simply making its cell empty? What are the drawbacks of the 'tombstone' solution?
reference_answer: A linear-probing search stops at an EMPTY cell, since an empty cell means the key was never placed further along. If element A is deleted by emptying its cell, a key B that collided and was placed after A can no longer be found — the probe chain is broken. Tombstone: mark the cell as 'deleted' — searches treat it as occupied and keep probing, while insertions can reuse it. Drawbacks: tombstones accumulate and lengthen probe chains, slowing searches (especially for absent keys) even when few real elements remain; periodic rehashing is needed to clean them, and the load factor must count tombstones. Alternative: backward-shift deletion (moving subsequent elements back to fill the gap) with linear probing.
key_points: Emptying a cell breaks probe chains, making keys placed after it unfindable
Tombstones preserve chains but accumulate and slow lookups; rehash periodically or use backward-shift deletion

subject: Data Structures and Algorithms
concept: Count-Min Sketch for approximate frequency counting
question: How does a Count-Min Sketch estimate element frequencies in a very large data stream? What properties does its error have?
reference_answer: A Count-Min Sketch is a d × w matrix of counters with d independent hash functions. When element x appears, for each row i increment the counter at column h_i(x). The frequency estimate for x is the MINIMUM of the counters h_i(x) over the d rows. Since other elements may collide into the same counters, each counter can only be greater than or equal to the true frequency, so the estimate never underestimates (only overestimates); taking the min over several rows reduces error. With w = ⌈e/ε⌉ and d = ⌈ln(1/δ)⌉, the error exceeds ε·N (N being the total number of elements) with probability at most δ. Memory depends only on ε and δ, not on the number of distinct elements — suited for counting URL hits and detecting heavy hitters in networks.
